newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong set to get leader-in-waiting this week.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong set to get leader-in-waiting this week.

text.p: The British colony of Hong Kong's drawn out transition to Chinese rule next year enters the home stretch on Wednesday when a handful of kingmakers meet to select the governor-in-waiting.
Three candidates have reached the final run-off. But the outcome is widely regarded in Hong Kong as a foregone conclusion.

Tycoon Tung Chee-hwa, 59, whose family shipping empire was bailed out by Beijing a decade ago, and who was singled out by China's president earlier in the year for a pointed and cordial handshake, is being touted as the chief executive-designate.

Nevertheless, 400 members of Hong Kong's new elite, carefully assembled by China, will gather in a cavernous convention centre on Wednesday and cast their vote in a process heralded by Beijing as the birth of true democracy here.
When July 1 breaks, the red flag of China will flutter over the last British outpost in Asia, a wealthy community of six million people to be governed by the man chosen this week.

The territory's pro-democracy lobby, which successfully spearheaded the battle against a benevolent but unrepresentative colonial administration, has angrily rejected Chinas claims it is bringing democracy to Hong Kong.
The Democratic Party, Hong Kong's largest, has branded the process to pick the future leadership a sham and boycotted it.
Activists picketed the first round of voting last month, presided over by China's Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who made his first visit to the British colony for the occasion.

"For the past 150 years, the governors appointed by Britain numbered more than 20-odd but did they ever consult the people of Hong Kong? Of course not," Qian told the 400-strong electoral panel seated in long rows before a raised dais.
Noisy protesters skirmished with police outside and attempted unsuccessfully to storm the building, site of the official handover ceremony next year.

Indoors, in scenes reminiscent of Communist Party plenums in Beijing's Great Hall of the People, the 400 members of the Selection Committee, an electoral college dominated by business tycoons actively wooed by Beijing, handed Tung a thumping victory in the first round of the vote.
Tung polled more than double the number of votes collected by his two rivals -- businessman Peter Woo, 50, and Yang Ti Liang, 67, Hong Kong's former chief justice.
After selecting the future leader, the committee's next task is to choose the Provisional Legislature which China plans to install in place of the existing elected chamber.

Work on this starts on Thursday in Shenzhen, just over the border in China, a sign that Beijing recognises the delicacy of establishing a rival body to the constitutionally-established chamber in Hong Kong.
It is this plan, the result of Chinese fury over democratic reforms presided over by the 28th and last British governor Chris Patten, that has divided politicians and power-brokers.

Britain, its allies in Europe and North America, and Hong Kong's democratic lobby, adamantly oppose dissolving the legislature because of the reforms, implemented in the twilight months of a colonial administration.

Some democrats say they are preparing to challenge the legality of the provisional legislature in court. Many of those who failed in the 1995 elections, the first under the Patten reforms, have applied to join the provisional legislature.
Tung was a senior and influential member of Patten's inner cabinet, the Executive Council, at the time of the reforms until he resigned this year to run for chief executive.
He has now publicly turned his back on the reforms and backed the Provisional Legislature. His caution appears to have paid dividends.
"Barring a last minute blunder, Tung Chee-hwa is set to be crowned Hong Kong's first chief executive on Wednesday," said the South China Morning Post's political editor, Chris Yeung.
